telegraphed them again saying that his personal and public honour was pledged to having the election on the same day and urging them to forward the writ. He said that notwithstanding that the writ was not issued in time to enable him to have the election on the same day, the argument being that there was no opportunity, when, as a matter of fact, the government themselves held back this writ against his wishes in order that they might have the advantage in that particular constituency of a deferred election. What is the feeling of the people of British Columbia in regard to this matter? Let us look at it from two or three phases that have not been mentioned. We have in this House 221 representatives from every portion of the Dominion and out of these 221 representatives there are seven from British Columbia, one at least of the greater provinces of this country. Of these seven representatives we had no less than three deferred elections, or, in other words, three sevenths of the entire electorate of British Columbia were practically disfranchised by deferred elections. I say that it is no wonder that the people of British Columbia felt indignant at the treatment that they received at the hands of this government. It is no wonder that they felt that they would resent such an injustice to them and to their province. That is one of the chief causes that led to the opposition to the government. But, there is another question that, it seems to me, enters into this. I believe that in deferring the elections in these various districts there is committed an injury to each particular district in which these elections are held. Let me illustrate: In Kootenay, which I have the honour to represent, as you know, in addition to the great mining industries that we have there, we have, in recent years, learned that the great valleys surrounding our lakes are suitable for fruit culture. Boards of trade and individuals have spent large sums of money in advertising the natural resources of that particular portion ot British Columbia and of its adaptability to horticulture. They have sent these advertisements all over Canada, to the old country and to the United States. They have been advertising these resources and the chief argument thej have advanced in regard to them was thai not only were these districts capable of growing all kinds of fruit of the best quality but that they were also close to the _ mar ket, that they had good railway facilities which would enable them to reach theii natural market, the prairies to the, east Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta Under these circumstances they were offer in<* inducements to people to come in ther< and settle the land. What was done? Jus at the time when Canada was engaged n a general election, when every newspape 90}	was devoting its front page and its editorial jolumns to the contest that was going on, just when the eyes of the mother country were focused upon the contest between the two great parties for the control of the affairs of this Dominion, it was announced that in certain portions of the province of British Columbia our means of communication were so backward that it was impossible to issue the writs and hold1 the elections on the same day as they were to be held in other parts of Canada. It did more harm *to the district of Kootenay and those portions of British Columbia in which we had deferred elections than will be offset by many years of hard work and a large expenditure of money. I do not hesitate to say that the people of these districts resented the position taken by the government with regard to these deferred elections. They felt that they had been dealt an unjust blow. They felt that all the work that had been done for years was undone by the position which these hon. gentlemen took with regard to this question. As to the position with regard to British Columbia I venture to say that it applies largely to other portions of the Dominion. In addition to the arguments which have been so logically advanced by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) I can only add that we have been unfairly dealt with in regard to advertising the great natural resources of that part of the Dominion. The time has come when we must show to the world at large that we have such good means of communication that all portions of the Dominion can be reached by the writs within the statutory time. It is a very important matter and one that affects every one of us. The country has spent large sums of money in making known its resources to other parts of the world. You find that the Minister of Agriculture and Minister of the Interior have spent large sums of money with regard to immigration and agriculture, advertising the great natural resources of the country and sending out agents at great cost, and yet, just at the time when a general election comes on, just at a time when we have an opportunity of advertising Canada, certain sections of the country are picked out and are un-fairlv dealt with by having it announced to the world that they are in such a backward position with regard to transportation facilities that elections cannot be held within these districts at the same time as they are held in other portions of the Dominion. I do not intend to take up the time of the House any longer with regard to this question. I believe that it has been fairly dealt with and I can only say t that this is not a resolution that has any i party advantage or object in view. I think * we have shown that the time has arrived

Although not myself the representative of a constituency in which deferred elections are held, as there are three constituencies ln, "e province *n, which that principle is adopted, it may be neecssary for me to give mv opinion on the question which is under discussion. Last session, when the question of deferred elections in British Columbia was being considered, like mv [DOT] fmiend,the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman), I thought that it might be possible to provide for having the election m the Kootenay district on the day of the general election. But, I had very grave doubts from the knowledge I had *fbrtgard t? Yale-Cariboo whether that wouid be possible there. I was absolutely certain that without some very serious change in the General Elections Act which \vould involve every constituency in Canada, it would be utterly impossible to provide for the Comox-Atlin district as the hon. minister has described to the House From the days of confederation in Canada, and owing to its peculiar and extensive geographical conditions, it has been considered necessary, on the part of both parties, that deferred elections should be neld. In England, as m- hon. friend from Yale-Canboo (Mr. Burrell) said, with its Mr. GOODEVE.	.
large centres of population, it has been considered necessary at certain periods to have deferred elections. The peculiar geographical conditions of Canada has necessitated all governments since confederation to defer the elections in certain constituencies.

Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that I contended that geography had anything to do with deferred elections in England? Surely he knows that the elections are not held on the same day in England because of the basis of the franchise which gives a man the right to vote in several constituencies where he is qualified?

I was stating that the conditions in this country gave far more reason for deferring elections than do the conditions in_ England. At all events all political parties since confederation have followed the same policy in that respect. My hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) based his whole argument against deferring elections on the beneficial results which he said would accrue to the candidate support-mg the party in power, but no stronger refutation of that argument can be found than the living presence of the hon. gentleman in this House. If the voters elect a man because he has charge of the flesh pots and can distribute them, and if a deferred election gives a government supporter great advantages in this respect, then the hon. gentleman would not represent the people of Yale-Cariboo in this House. The c ^ H^ritleman said he preferred the system of having the general elections on a fixed date which incidentally of course would mean that each parliament would be elected to sit for a specified and fixed term. Well that is a proposed change in the British constitution which I am not prepared to subscribe to.
I did not say I preferred that system ; I merely said there were arguments in favo uf of it ;as there were arguments against it.

Under the principles of the British representative constitution which we have incorporated into the constitution of Canada, the people of this country can at any time they find good reason for doing so turn out the government in power. Seven days after they have voted to put a certain party in power, they may, under :thq elasticity of the British system turn that party out of power again; but, under the United States system, which is less democratic, they elect their representatives for four years, and for four years whether the policy of the Congress may be approved by the people or not, the men so elected remain at the head of the nation. I am entirely opposed' to that

system. Now, as to deferring elections, I agree that so far as it is possible we should hold all the elections in Canada on the same day. The hon. gentleman calls upon me to vote non-confidence in the government because they have, as all former Canadian governments have, deferred elections in certain constituencies Well, even supposing the government is wrong in that, surely we can find a remedy without voting against a good government which in other respects has done so much to advance the material interests of the people of this country. Even though I should disagree with the government in regard to one particular item in their policy, and that certainly not a very important one in comparison with others, I would be very loth indeed to Vote against them on all questions because I might disagree with them on one point. I believe this debate will have a tendency to influence this government, and all future governments, to reduce the number of deferred elections to the narrowest possible limit. I said a year ago in this House that I believed it was not necessary to defer the election in Kootenay. My hon. friend from that constituency (Mr. Goodeve) has told us that tbe government candidate denounced the provision for a deferred election and stated in his election address that he preferred that the election should be on the same day as the general elections and we are told that on account of the alleged unnecessary and unreasonable deferring of the election a great many of the voters in these British Columbia constituencies voted against the government. It is quite evident, if this be true, that the Liberal party had no political motive in having a deferred election. If the Liberals of these districts and the government candidates for these districts were against deferred elections, how can my hon. friend say that there was any political motive in holding the deferred election? I believe the people of these constituencies generally do think that provision could be made to have the elections on the same day. Personally, I think it would be very difficult in Yale-Cariboo; it may be possible in Kootenay; I think it is impossible in Comox-Atlin. I am convinced that there are geographical conditions because of which, unless there is a very radical change in the law, it will be impossible to apply the rule of simultaneous elections in some of the constituencies for some years to come.

' It certainly is interesting to note that two very intelligent men on the other side of the House, the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Fielding), and Mr. Ralph Smith (Vancouver), could have persuaded themselves that they had convinced each other that this was a vote of want of confidence. If the hon. member for Vancouver
was convinced by the argument of the Minister of Finance that this was a vote of want of confidence, does he accept the necessary conclusion that every amendment to Supply is a vote of want of confidence and that to vote for such an amendment is to vote against the government?
I would ask the hon. member (Mr. Foster), in return, if it is possible for me to have my views expressed in the form of an amendment to this motion.

That is not the point. The hon. member (Mr. Ralph Smith) said that one of his reasons for not wanting to vote for this resolution was that he does not want to turn out a good government, notwithstanding the fact that, so far as the proposal in that amendment is concerned, it ought to be carried out if possible. The Minister of Finance rather surprised me by making the statement in the categorical way he did. He not only said this was a vote of want of confidence, but that the only method by which a vote of want of confidence could be moved was by amendment to a motion for Supply. I do not think he really believes that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the most common way.

But the minister did not say that; he said it was the only way, and he called upon his supporters, in as clear terms as he could use, to vote against this amendment because it was a motion of want of confidence. My hon. friend from Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) has cited seven or eight instances of amendments to Supply accepted by the government and carried unanimously, some moved on the government side, and some moved on the opposition side. Such instances occur almost every session.
We had two last session.

Yes, we had two last session as my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) observes. Common sense is against regarding such an amendment as necessarily a vote of want of confidence, and all parliamentary practice is against it. A motion of want of confidence is defined by what the motion itself contains. If my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) were to move that the administration of the Minister of Finance had been corrupt and wasteful and therefore unworthy of confidence, that would be a clear motion of want of confidence, and it would not make a bit of difference whether it was moved in amendment to Supply or as an independent motion. I quite agree that, if the ministry wish, they can declare any motion to be a motion of want of confidence, and call upon their followers to treat it as such. In such a case it is for the independent minds behind the

Treasury benches to decide whether it is a vote of want of confidence or not and also how they shall declare themselves Concerning it.
Another point that has been made is that the amendment should not be passed because there are details which would make it impossible to carry it out except after amendment of the law. As my hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve) has pointed out, this is simply the declaration of a principle, a principle which has been accepted, in the main, by the Minister of Finance himself, by the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman), by the member for Nanaimo and by all the others who have spoken on the other side of the House. As this is merely a declaration of principle, if there are details to be arranged in' order to carry it out, those details can be considered after. This would be a mere expression of opinion of the House, an in* struction to the government, that the principle ought to be carried out; it would be for legislation to come in afterwards and make the merely mechanical re-arrangements with respect to time and distance to carry the principle into effect.
But I wish to call attention to an argument upon which the hon. member for Nanaimo seemed to plume himself a good deal. He said that the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell} was a living demonstration that the position he took was not a valid position. It is true, I suppose, that dynamite exploded in proximity to a man is apt to damage the man. It is also true that a case may be found where the discharge has gone in another direction, so that the man, though apparently in imminent danger, has escaped damage. Would the hon. member (Mr. Ralph Smith) contend that because, in one case the man had escaped, that that was an argument against being careful about leaving dynamite around where it may explode when some unoffending citizen of this counary is near at hand? That was an argument used by my hon. friend from Vancouver which did not do him justice. He can make better arguments than that. But he has been up against it this afternoon; in order to find a reason to vote for the government he had to have recourse to an argument like that. If, now and again, a constituency rises superior to the influence of a deferred election, if a constituency, outraged by the continual application of this method decides that it will take the bit in its teeth, and, government or no government, will vote emphatic denial of such a principle, can that be considered an argument in favour of deferred elections? Because that happens now and then, is it an argument that you can use those things and should use them, and that the abuse should not be taken away. But the thing underlying that, and my hon. friend knows Mr. FOSTER.
it well, is this: is it proper, when it is not necessary to have a deferred election, for the government to defer it and thus better use the kind of argument used in these constituencies. That is the principle which is under it, and my hon. friend is too intelligent and straightforward to stand for a thing of that kind. But what does he think of the action of his own government? The two candidates, Liberal and Conservative, who knew their constituency, who knew their geographic limitations, came to a compact and agreed that they did not want any deferred election but a fair, straight combat in the ring without any handicap. The Liberal candidate both wrote and wired his government to give a square contest on the day when everybody else was casting his ballot in the Dominion. But your Finance Minister and your Prime Minister, whom you do not want to turn out and censure, rode rough-shod over him and said: You shall not have a fair fight, but we will put a handicap in your favour, and will do it by means of a deferred election. There was not a word of reprobation of an act like that by my hon. friend. He is so anxious to stand at the back of the Minister of Inland Revenue and support his loins, his arms, his shoulders and his head, that he would not reprove the wrong action for fear he would cause some damage by imputation to that heaven-sent minister.

When the House rose I was dealing with some arguments adduced by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith). I always listen with pleasure and interest to what the member for Nanaimo (Mr. R. Smith) says. He is a man of wide experience, a man who thinks for himself and who appears to be exceedingly well informed on a wide range of subjects. I have heard him make most excellent arguments in this House. Of course it is difficult for a man to make a good argument if he has a poor case, and I attribute the weakness of his argument this afternoon to the poor case he had to defend. The member for Nanaimo (Mr. R. Smith) has won his spurs. He has conquered his constituency, he has kept it after conquering it; in many a hard fight he has proved the winner. After the election of 1908 he came here with his spurs on. I cannot say quite the same of the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman). The Minister of Inland Revenue did not quite win his spurs in the same way as the member for Nanaimo. It strikes me that some years ago there was something of a deal by the transference to the Senate of a par-

ticular person to give him a seat in this House and enable him to enter the cabinet. He entered the Cabinet without portfolio, but afterwards became a full-fledged minister. In the election of 1908, like many another good man, he went down before the wrath of the people and he is now here by virtue of another arrangement. The el-elcted member for Comox-Atlin, the man who fought the contest, who stood at the polls and took the battle upon him, came out victorious and came here as a full-fledged member of this House. It seems that there must be sacrifice somewhere and in some way or other the sacrifice was accomplished and the Minister of Inland Revenue, by way of Mr. Sloan, sits in this House to-day. So I say that for a man who has won his spurs in many a hard fought battle, who has fought consistently and always in his own consituency. it must come a little hard and it must be from a high sense of public duty that he stands so loyally to the back of the minister and his colleagues. The member for Nanaimo (Mr. R. Smith) I think has good cabinet material in him, he had won his position and might well have looked for preferment when preferment was possible; but instead of that the member for Nanaimo is not recognized and a deal is made by which the Minister of Inland Revenue gets into this House. I was interested this afternoon when the Minister of Inland Revenue was making his argument. He told the House plainly that if there had been an election contest in Comox-Atlin large numbers of electors would have been disfranchised. Did the minister have it so arranged that he knew from the first there was going to be no election. Suppose that, contrary to his supposition, if he had any in that respect, some obdurate man had been found in Comox-Atlin who would have stood at the polls and have forced a contest; by the admission of my hon. friend himself a large number of people in Comox-Atlin would have been disfranchised. By whose action? By his own action. Before he left Ottawa he and his government had arranged exactly what time should be given and they so arranged the time that if in the natural course of things there had been an election a large number of residents and electors in his own constituency would have been disfranchised. Myhon. friend this afternoon deplored anything of the kind. He is in favour of deferred elections lest perchance somebody in a constituency shall be disfranchised and yet he and his government set the whole machinery into operation by virtue of which, if there had been an election, hundreds of his own constituents would not have had a chance to vote. The only supposition that will reconcile the minister's actions with his expressed desire that no one should be disfranchised, is
that from the first, when fixing the dates and arranging the machinery, he had a pretty good idea that there was going to be no_eiection.
Now we come to the argument of the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) who declared that in Gaspe it was physically impossible to hold the elections on the same date as the general elections, provided all the machinery was exactly as it is now. What were the arguments he used? Two hundred and fifty miles of an extension, but that is not insuperable in these times and finally the Postmaster General himself admitted that it would be possible to hold the elections on the mainland of Gaspe on the date of the general election, but he thought it might not be possible, under certain circumstances, on the Magdalen Islands. Yet the Magdalen Islands have complete telegraphic communication with the mainland. He was afraid there might be some possible mistake in a date in transmitting the telegram to the Magdalen Islands. It is the simplest thing in the world to have a telegram repeated so that _ the man sending it knows that it is received exactlv as he sent it. Thus, by his own admission, it would be possible to carry out the general law. What is the kernel of the whole matter ? It is the urging of a lot of technical and easily removed objections in order to retain a system which it is acknowledged by all should be abandoned if it is possible to do without it. _
Now on the cne side, what is it? Technicalities, geographical difficulties, mechanical difficulties and the like of that; on the other side, an acknowledged grievance an acknowledged disability, an acknowledged bad method. Will any one stand up in ohis House and aTgue for a single moment that a deferred election is fair between man and man as candidates in a contest? I do not think any one will. In a contest where the whole Dominion is engaged upon public issues, public men on each side go into the contest and they have a fair field so far as it can be given to them. Each one has the right to argue and instil into the minds of the electors that his party is the best party, has the best methods, and will likely rule the country for the next four or five, years. Each stands on a level. It depends on the men which of the two shall be the better persuader of his audience. But when you put a deferred election on, and you have the issue already decided in the Dominion, and it is no longer a question as to which party shall be in power for the next five years, no man*can say that it is a fair fight as between man and man. Don't we believe in fair fighting? _ Whatever government is in power, does it want to keep in power by unfair fighting? Does it want to load the dice? Surely not. Then I say I that one of the great evils of a deferred elec-

tion is that it does not play the game fairly, it handicaps one man in favour of another, and he the nominee of the government.
I say it is not only unfair between man and man but it is unfair between party and party. Go into a general election contest, even though we use those methods which we deplore, suppose the government candidate says: If you want public works in your constituency you had better elect me, for my party is going to be in power. The man who listens to him looks up in his face and says: Well, that is yet to be tested, you don't know, and we are not at all sanguine that your party will be in power. The candidate on the other side gets up and says: Vote for me, for my party, and for my party's policy; and he meets the argument of the other man by saying: I believe that my party will be in power, and that consequently we will have rule in the Dominion for the next four or five years. You put the two parties on as fair and equal footing for the fight as you can. But make it a deferred election, and what do you do? You handicap one party entirely, so far as you can, you read it out of any chance or hope of being successful in the election contest, because they are up against an issue which is decided already in the country. So it is not fair between party and party. I hold that no matter what a party may gain by that kind of thing, in the long run it loses if it offends the principles of fair play and just warfare as between the two great parties in the country. Some time or other it will come back on them. It hits first one party and then another, if it is carried on. But it is not good for either party. .
But there is a higher issue than that. It defrauds the elector in the deferred constituency of any chance of deciding the public issues of the day. What is the whole theory of our free and responsible government? It is that by aggregating the units of voices throughout the whole country you get a proper conclusion as to the policy which shall rule the country. Is it not essential, then, that the contest should be carried on under conditions which give to each man a chance to have a voice in deciding the final issue? Your deferred election takes away that chance from the man in the minority party, and the moment he presents his policy he is told, the issue is already decided, and you have a matter of public policy in which the voter has no chance at all to decide what it will be, it has already been decided, and it is a dead issue in that constituency. Now what is the effect of that? What do we want in this country, dead constituencies or live constituencies? Is it best that we should have the finest spirit, is it best that we should have the liveliest and keenest discussion, is it best that we should have the energies of all the electors devoted to the solution of ques-Mr. FOSTER.
tions that come before them? Evidently so. But by the deferred election you destroy that liveliness, you destroy that independent participation, and you throw a dead issue into that constituency, and consequently you do what militates directly against public spirit, and the better public life of that constituency and of the country at large. It is not right, and it is not expedient. It is not right, because it deprives the elector of his proper position; it is not expedient, because in the long run it discourages public spirit and is a disadvantage to the country.
Well, then do we agree upon that? I ask the Finance Minister, in the way of reasoning this out, do we agree that it is not a desirable thing to go into any con-situency and to try to get a vote by the bold promise of public works and of public patronage? No man, I think, will get up in this House and argue on that brute idea. He will hedge about it, even though he believes that he or his party will use that kind of an instrumentality, he will not advocate it baldly and boldly. The issues of the day, the discussion of these great public issues, the great public policies, the interests of the country at large, these are the things which should be discussed in the election, and to leave those aside and to replace them by, or give greater prominence to, the brute arguments and promises of what the government will do in the bestowal of money, and franchises, and public works, and that kind of thing, debauches the constituency. It is a course which is deleterious, nobody can stand up in this twentieth century, and go in for and advocate that sort of thing. But your deferred election gives force and power to that argument. The two men on a platform in a general election have a fair show, neither can say that his party is in, or that his principles will triumph. But in a deferred election a government is in, that government has the patronage, that government dispenses the money- Vote for me, or you will get nothing for your constituency in any way, shape or form. That is the bald argument used over and over again. It is used with tremendous force when all are fighting on the same day, it is used with tenfold more force when you defer an election and you give to one party or to one candidate pcwer to say: ' We are in for five years, we dispense the patronage, we build the post offices, we appoint the officers, we do all that sort of thing, and you will not get a smell of patronage unless you vote for me. The government will be kind to its friends.*' My good natured friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), says that is human nature, and that every party will always be more favourable to its friends. Another puts it in a different way.

and so we have it. But when it is put so baldly as that, and in a deferred election, even my good natured and human friend, the Minister of Railways, would, I think, rather balk at that kind of a statement in its bareness and its foulness, I do not think he would stand at the back of that. Therefore, I say that the deferred election is the enemy of the country, of the commonwealth, of good public life, because it gives the greatest possible force to the worst kind of arguments, the argument of patronage, when a man says, 'I belong to the party which is going to exercise this patronage for the next five years, make me your man and I will get these expenditures in your constituency.' What have you on the other side? You have, on the other side, simply what has been urged here this afternoon, that there are geographical difficulties in the way. You will have to use the telegraph; in some cases you will have to send couriers out; in other cases you will have to have this, do this and that as a mechanical expedient in order to expedite the work to have everything made ready for the decision on polling day. What are these things?-simply technicalities, little mechanical difficulties which, if it were determined that the principle shall triumph, we are abundantly able in half an hour to meet by legislation. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) has shown how it can be met in Comox-Atlin and he has held up Comox-Atlin as a conspicuous example of a large and unwieldy constituency. That situation can be met by making the proclamation two weeks in advance. We are competent to meet that by legislation. It is the easiest possible thing in the world to do. If we want to establish this principle we can easily smooth out all these little mechanical difficulties and put the matter where it ought to be. But, remembering the illustration given by my hon. friend (Mr. Goodeve), I am afraid that the real reason why the deferred constituency is kept is that the government itself is favourable to it and does not want to relinquish the hold it gives. It will not hurt us to give that illustration once more before I stop talking on this phase of the subject. What was it? The Liberal candidate in Kootenay wanted no deferred election, the Conservative candidate wanted none, and the two, like brothers in a good, square, fair fight agree that there should be none. What happens?-the candidate of the government wires to the government; 'I want the election on the regular day.' He writes to the government:	'Please set the election
on the regular day.' The government do not. Why not? Not because it is not feasible or practicable, but because it wants to handicap the man who is opposed to it and give an advantage to the
man who is running in its interests. So long as that is the spirit of the government no wonder the Minister of Finance strains every constitutional and reasonable principle and declares that an amendment like this involves a vote of want of confidence and calls upon his followers to vote against it. No wonder that my self-sacrificing friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) treats it, on the ipse dixit of the Minister of Finance, as being a vote of -want of confidence and says:	'I do not want to turn
out this good government: better a thousand deferred elections and all that they involve than that this government that I support should go out.' There it is. It is up to parliament just now to say whether or' not we will adopt the principle which we all believe to be correct and then set ourselves to smoothing away the difficulties in the way of carrying it into actual practice, or whether we .will go on in the old wav. the way which accentuates the difficulties that we are strong enough to overcome now in the political life of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion on both sides of the House on the question of deferred elections. According to the speech made by the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) one would imagine that it was a Conservative candidate who in all cases suff.ered by deferred elections. I happen to represent a constituency in which I was the sufferer, and not only that, but a large proportion of the constituency was disfranchised by reason of the fact that the election was not deferred. I may say that although the member for Yale-Cariboo may think that he put the question, as it appeared to him, fairly, it must be remembered that there are other places in Canada as well as Yale-Cariboo. There are districts probably as large and just as hard to get over as the constituency my hon. friend represents. I have the honour to represent a constituency extending from the city of Edmonton to, you may say, the North Pole. I wish to inform the House that although there is a large settlement north of the Athabaska river there was no poll in my constituency north of that river. Some hon. gentlemen might think that there was a desire on the part of the Liberals in the late election to act unfairly and that there was some motive for not placing a poll north of the river, but, I want to point out that the district of Athabaska is represented in the Local House at Edmonton by a Liberal. He was elected by acclamation. I think I know the people in that country probably better than any man in the House, if not as well as any man in the Northwest, and I do not know the name of one Conservative north of that

river. I know that there are over 300 votes in. that region and that we only had to place a poll there to secure those votes. The Liberal associations at Fort McMur-ray and Fort Smith applied for a poll but the government did not see their way clear to establish one although I, as the rep-presentative of the party in the recent contest, was very anxious to have one placed in that district. We could not get it and the result was that a large portion of the constituency was disfranchised. I would be sorry to see this occur again. I hope that in the next election these people will have an opportunity of casting their votes. Unless there are great changes which we do not now expect, such as the extension of railways into that north country, when the next election comes on these people will be in exactly the same position as that which they occupied in the last election. I think it is unfair that such a large proportion of the electors should be disfranchised and I am therefore very much opposed to the resolution doing away with the deferred elections while there are voters in remote corners of any constituency who do not have an opportunity to vote. My opponent in the late election was very anxious with regard to this matter. His agent approached me and said he hoped they would not place any poll in that country. His agent tried to make an arrangement with me which, of course, I had no authority to make, his reason being that it was impossible to go up there. If a poll had been placed there I would have had a great advantage over my opponent. The local member who .is a friend of mine would have looked after my interests there while my opponent had no chance of sending anybody in and I would undoubtedly have secured the_ vote. If these people are disfranchised in the next election I do not think they well be very well satisfied, I do not think they should be, and I promised them that I would do all in my power to secure to them in the next election the opportunity of casting their votes the same as the voters in any other part of the district. I have only to add that I will vote against the resolution in the interest of constituencies which would suffer if there were no deferred elections.

Mr. Speaker. I shall endeavour to make my remarks fittingly brief, and in the first place I shall touch upon the observations made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). The major part of the hon. gentleman's speech was devoted to jeering at the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith), and at the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue. He takes exception to the manner in which the Minister of Inland Revenue finds a seat in this House.

It is true that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Templeman) was defeated by a narrow majority at the recent elections, and it is also true that he was defeated by most despicable means. I for one who support the government am here to say that when we remember the means by which the Minister of Inland Revenue was defeated, he has not the slightest fallen in our estimation, but on the contrary we think the more of him. It is true, as the hon. member for North Toronto has said, that in 1906 the Minister of Inland Revenue found a seat in this House because of a vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Riley, now a senator. The people of the city in which the Minister of Inland Revenue lives were glad to elect him on that occasion and they would have been glad to have elected him on the 26th of October last if _ they had not been misled and deceived. But, when we look at the records of how the Minister of Inland Revenue has found a seat in this House and of how the hon. member for North Toronto has found a seat here, I do not think the comparison is very much to the credit of my hon. friend from North Toronto. I had rather be in the position of the Minister of Inland Revenue who found a seat in the city in which he lived for many years and of which he is one of the pioneers, known and respected, than be in the position of the hon. member for North Toronto who, I am informed, started his political career in a place called the County of Kings in the province of New Brunswick down by the sea. I am told that from there he went to another county ; he wandered to and fro on the earth, and he found a lodging place in the county of York
Mr. Speaker, I ask, has this anything to do with the question before the House.
Sit down.
Order. I will hear the hon. gentleman on the point of order.
I ask has this anything to do with the question under consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I submit that it has as much to do with it as the speech of my hon. friend from North Toronto.
You don't mean that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do.
My point of order is that the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) are not pertinent to the subject under discussion, and I ask your ruling.

The motion is that the House go into Committee of Supply, and on that motion considerable latitude is allowed. There is an amendment relating to deferred elections, and as I have allowed considerable latitude to the mover of that

amendment I think I would not now be justified in restricting the scope of the debate.

My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) next went to the city of St. John, and he again was a candidate. There was no doubt good reason why he left the county of York, but there was no good reason evidently for his going to St. John, because he was defeated there by the late Hon. Mr. Blair who polled an overwhelming majority. Then, my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) went forth wandering to and fro on the earth, seeking whom he might
Devour.

Seeking whom he might represent, and in the course of time he came to the riding of North Ontario, in the old province of Ontario. He ran against a young man, a little more than out of his teens, and my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) with all his record behind him-I don't say because of his record, but perhaps I may be more courteous and say in spite of his record-with all his experience, with all his ability, with all his prestige as a prominent member if not the leader of the once great Conservative party; he went down to defeat before this boy, George Grant. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) tried again at the general election of 1904, and he went to that citv of Toronto where even the hon. gentleman can be elected, since he is a Conservative. I will admit this with regard to my hon. friend:	He may be
against deferred elections because he experienced great deferring of his own election on that occasion ; time after time for four years his election was deferred_ and the. expression ' deferred election ' is, I have no doubt, one which makes the hon. gentleman anything but pleasant. Let me remind the hon. gentleman that while he was a member of the Conservative government, I think for some _ eleven years, there was a general election in 1887, another in 1891, and another in 1896. During all this period the hon. gentleman was a prominent member of the Conservative government, a clever member, and I have no doubt a worthy member so far as I have any knowledge. But in each of these three elections the government of which the hon. gentleman was a member were responsible foT deferred elections, and for these he must share the responsibility. It it only fair that I should say that he has by supporting the policy of the government of which he was a member admitted that deferred elections are not in theinselves wrong, but are necessities, and justifiable under certain circumstances, or else of course he would not have supported his government. I have before me the Consolidated Statutes of Canada for the year 1886, and I find set forth in the Elections
Act a list of constituencies in which there should be deferred elections and these constituencies are the electoral district of Al-goma, the electoral district of Gaspe, the electoral district of Chicoutimi and Saguenay, and would the House believe it, every one of the electoral districts in the province of British Columbia. That is the law which was in force when my hon. friend was a member of the government, and it is only fair we should come to the conclusion that to-day he cannot consistently lay down the policy that deferred elections are in themselves never justifiable. Mv hon. friend (Mr. Foster) referred specially to the fact that Mr. Smith Curtis, the Liberal candidate in Kootenay, was desirous of having the election upon the same day as the other elections throughout the country. My hon. friend told us twice that the two candidates were desirous of standing up like brothers in a friendly fight, and say to each other:	'We
will have nothing mean, we will fight thi3 thing out fair.' By that, of course, he implies that the government endeavoured in the province of British Columbia to use underhand methods, and I have no doubt he in some way endeavoured to cast the asperations on the Liberal party for the manner in which they fought the elections in that province:	I want to say that we
have no need to sit at the feet of gentlemen opposite to learn how to conduct elections in British Columbia. It has been stated by some gentlemen that because an election is deferred, there is therefore a greater probability that the people will be unduly influenced to vote for the party in power. To my mind that is not a compliment to the people of British Columbia. The hon. gentleman from Yale-Cariboo has said that in England it is different because conditions are different, and that the electorate there are not susceptible to the influence of the government in power. I think that on reflection the hon. gentleman will withdraw^ the invidious comparison as between his own constituents and the voters in the British Isles because I believe it will be found that the electors of the Dominion of Canada and the electors of British Columbia are just as competent to give a fair and unprejudiced vote on political affairs as are the voters in England, Ireland, or Scotland.
Only one case can I recall in which the people were ready to lay aside their allegiance to the principles of their party and support the Liberal party because it was in power, and that was the case of the Te-cent by-election in which the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) was elected. On that occasion, we found the Conservatives of Victoria, we found the Conservatives of Vancouver, so disgusted 1 with the election methods of their party

last October, that they came out flat-footed and said: 'To show that we are ashamed of this system by which our party has disgraced us, let us call for the withdrawal of the man who has been put up in Prince Rupert. True, we elected Conservatives in October last, but we did so because we were deceived by forged telegrams, but now we know better.' And the result was that against his own -wishes, and by the influence and pressure of the Conservatives in Victoria and Vancouver, he was withdrawn from the contest. And so these people to that extent, redeemed themselves and paid this compliment to the hon. minister. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) tried to make is appear that the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith) had, so to speak, swallowed himself on this question. The hon. member for Nanaimo does (pV require that I -should hold any brief for him. He has been many years in this House, and. no member of this House is held in higher esteem. He is not the man to disguise his principles, nor can he fittingly be made the subject of such remarks as those of the hon. member for North Toronto. My hon. friend {M Foster) also jeered at the hon. member for Nanaimo because in this instance he had been loyal to the Minister of Inland Revenue-'this heaven-born minister,' as the non. gentleman said, with some sarcasm,
I suppose. I will admit-nay, I will claim - that it is quite possible "that the hon. member for North Toronto may not be able to understand loyalty to colleagues nor to the minister; we have heard of the 'nest of traitors.' To him, it may be a passing mystery, which he can only treat sarcastically as something that he cannot understand, that the hon. member for Nanaimo and other Liberal members who support this government have in their hearts an honest loyalty to the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) as to every other member of the ministry. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) was greatly exercised about the power of patronage-that the poor innocent elector should be misled or unduly influenced by the expectation that, since a certain party is in power certam things will be done. That is something that would never be practised by the hon. member for North Toronto while in "'is House. Does he remember a trip -that he made to Prince Edward Island? Did he ever hear of the building of a tunnel to Prince Edward Island? I am not going into the merits or demerits of that remarkable construction that was proposed; but I will say that I do not think it is any worse for candidates to say frankly to their electors that if they are returned to parliament their constituents will have the sympathy and ear of the government in presenting their petitions, than to hold forth to the people Mr. KNOWLES.
of Prince Edward Island the prospect that if the leader of the opposition is brought into power a tunnel will be built. I am not saying that I defend this style of electioneering, at all, but I say that the first of these is better than the other.
With regard to the specific matters that have been spoken of, if I understand my hen. friend from Yale-Cariboo, he himself admitted that it would require twelve days to'Teach certain parts of his district. I submit, there can be no justification for disfranchising these people who are twelve days' journey removed from the centres of population. These people have all the rights of franchise that people living in the city of Vernon have, or in the town of Grand Forks, or in the city of Kamloops, or in the city of Nelson. The principle which he himself declared for, this afternoon, the principle that nobody should be disfranchised, should cause the hon. gentleman to rise to-night and vote against his own motion, because he himself has shown that to do away with deferred elections means that you must disfranchise many hundreds of people in this Dominion. I think we had that very clearly demonstrated this afternoon by my hon. friend Lorn Prince Albert (Mr. Rutan), whom I am very happy to see here. That hon. gentleman has demonstrated to this House that in his own riding there are seven polls where 228 votes were cast, which are from 250 to 500 miles from the city of Prince Albert, where, of course, the returning officer would almost necessarily live. That journey is made partly by pumping a hand car to the Pas, partly by portaging, and by hundreds of miles of canoeing up stream. That journey cannot be made in one day less than two weeks. And, away up there, there are about 250 people who have as much right to vote as the people of Prince Albert have. I was for ten days occupied in assisting my hon. friend from Prince Albert in that election, and I never met a single Conservative who seriously said there was any injustice in that deferred election. On the other hand, Conservative after Conservative admitted that it would have been an injustice and an outrage that these 228 votes should not have been cast, for the people in those remote sections had as good a right to cast their ballots as the people in the centres. We are not afraid of the polls in the cities nor those far removed. We say: 'Let all the people in all parts of the country have the opportunity to exercise their franchise.' Another illustration is that in the Dominion constituency of Edmonton there are two local provincial constituencies, Athabaska and Peace River. In the recent general election, because they did not have deferred elections, in the provincial constituency of Athabaska only_ one poll was held, and in the provincial constituency of Peace River, not

a single vote was polled, poll was held, or vote cast, because these British subjects were too far removed from the place of polling, and therefore could not exercise their franchise. In my own riding there were nine polls that could not be held, and were not held. If they had been held, I think, beyond question, I should have had a majority of 150 more. I do not say that to boast, but lest any person should think that there was purpose in not holding these polls. I see my hon. friend laughing sarcastically. My majority was over 1,000, so that I would not have been in danger even had these polls gone against me. If we had had a deferred election these votes would have been _ polled. The application of the very principle which my hon. friend (Mr. Burrell) asks this House to adopt, resulted, in the riding of Edmonton, in the disfranchisement of two provincial constituencies, and in my own riding it resulted in the disfranchisement of at least nine polls. There was one poll where they made their own ballot box, and their own poll, and cast seven solid Liberal votes. They wanted to vote for good government, but they had not the chance. Therefore I say that the people living in the outlying parts of the prairie should be protected; and instead of the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr Burrell) and his associates in this debate endeavouring to further take away from that franchise, they would be much better employed if they would take better precautions to prevent the disfranchising of these electors.
Instead of having to apologize for the vote I propose to give, I should, if I voted for the principle contained in this resolution, be absolutely wrong. Let us bear in mind the circumstances and conditions which existed when the decision was arrived at to have deferred elections. It is well known that if a person is charged with wrong-doing, you must consider his conduct from the view point of the circumstances at the time he did the alleged wrong. It is said that we did wrong in deferring the elections. Before deciding, let us consider what were the circumstances which induced the government to defer them. According to the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite, the decision to defer the elections could only be wrong if thereby the return of the government was rendered more likely than its overthrow. But which was the more likely at the time ? My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in an interview which he gave the press a few days before the general election, said that they would be a repetition of the general elections of 1878. Surely then he must have been convinced that the deferring of certain elections, if the result was to be in favour of the government, would have the effect of returning the Conservative candidates, since the general
elections were to be a repetition of those of 1878 and the Conservative party be in power. The offense must be judged from the view point of the circumstances that existed at the time the wrong was committed; and since the circumstances then pointed to the overthrow of the Liberal government and party, the Liberal party stood to lose and not to gain by deferring these elections, and therefore the deferring of them was a kindness done the opposition, because after sweeping the country the opposition could come in and gather a few more crumbs.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. H. BARNARD (Victoria, British Columbia).
speechtext:
It was not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to take any part in this debate until I heard from the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Knowles), He saw fit in his wisdom to dilate upon the circumstances of the election in the city of Victoria and to cast some animadversion on the Liberal-Conservative party in respect to that election and to profess a great deal of sympathy foT the Minister of Inland Revenue over its results. Hon. gentlemen opposite have, during the present session, seen fit on more than one occasion to refer to that election in terms in themselves somewhat amusing, and for my part I was perfectly content they should so amuse themselves if they saw fit. It was not my intention or desire to lay before the House the facts concerning the career of the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue, (Mr. Templeman), as regards elections in the city of Victoria, so long as hon. gentlemen opposite confined themselves to their little, pleasantries. But when they take part in a serious debate and raise that question in a wholly irrelevant manner, it seems to me high time that I should say something on the subject.
As regards the incident referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Knowles) I had nothing to do with it, and am as innocent of any connection with it as the hon. gentleman himself. Last year about July 15th, the question of the piers built at Riviere du Moulin, was brought up before the House. Well, I may be allowed to refer to the explanations which I gave to this House last year on July 15th. Let me remind him of some photographs which I laid before this House last year showing the piers of the bridge at Grande Decharge, Lake Saint John, the building of which he himself authorized when Finance Minister in 1894, at the request of his colleague, the Hon. Mr. Ouimet, then Minister of Public Works, an achiev-ment of which he was quite proud, as a means of making friends in my district. If the Conservatives deemed it right and equitable and honourable to appropriate moneys from the federal chest for the building of piers as part of a bridge to help along colonization in the Lake Saint John district, a work wholly of provincial interest, is this government to be condemned for having done this very thing, admitting that they have done so, which I deny. True, this government have allowed the appropriation as made to appear openly in the public accounts; while, as evidence of the help contributed towards the building of that bridge in Lake St. John, the Department of Colonization at Quebec was called upon to give a voucher under the signature of Mr. Dufault, deputy minister, acknowledging the receipt of $2,000 as grant towards the building of the bridge.
If those hon. gentlemen who have criticised so loudly yesterday were to come to Chicoutimi and repeat their utterances, thev might be surprised at the warm reception they would have at the hands especially of the farmers who signed the petition requesting that these works be undertaken and setting forth reasons in support.

taking a certain Simon Lapointe, who approached some of them a couple of weeks ago as the authorized representative of the Conservative party in my constituency. I notice in his seat the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Price). I may say that I infinitely regret for the sake of his prestige among his numerous friends inhabiting my constituency that he should have thought fit to countenance this farce. True, this woodwork to which he referred and which is still in existence, was put in originally by Price Brothers. Nobody denies it or has ever thought of denying it. But if my hon. friend is conversant with the history of his firm, to the same extent as are the people of Chicoutimi, he will be bound to acknowledge that this woodwork was put in at the time in order to prevent the washing away by the waters of the Saguenay, and through the action of frost, of the strip of land which it incloses; and as a matter of fact, wherever the old woodwork is broken down, the shore is eaten up from year to year through the action of

those two factors I have just mentioned. In the near future, these old protection works have fallen to pieces, it will be necessary to renew them; otherwise this piece of land will be washed out in the same v.ay as higher up along the course of the river, the most fertile lands of the parish of Sainte-Anne are yearly being eaten up by the waters of the Saguenay.
As further evidence of the beneficent and effective part played by the government on that occasion, I may state that while, in 1904, there was a large majority of votes polled against me, both in the town and parish of Chicoutimi, in 1908, there was a large majority of votes polled in my favour, although during the election strenuous efforts had been made in Chicoutimi by the Lapointe gang, with a view to securing the express condemnation of the policy pursued by the government in the shape of a large hostile vote which was loudly announced in advance.
The pier referred to was built at the request of the citizens of Chicoutimi, who forwarded a petition bearing numerous signatures of farmers and leading business men of the locality, and urging that the building of such a pier would be a safeguard for years to come, and the beginning of a great work destined to replace the wooden structure previously referred to. The officers of the department have taken the same view; and I contend that no hon. member in this House has the right to insinuate that the minister, the government and the House have been basely deceived in this connection, and that accordingly the officers of the department have acted wrongly. The department deserves credit for the building of this pier both as a work of art and utility, and as time goes by, it will be found, and before long, perhaps, that the insinuations of party politicians in this connection have no foundation in fact, and were inspired by motives other than public interest.
In conclusion, I return to what I said a while ago. Even admitting that this pier was built expressly to support a bridge, I cannot conceive why hon. gentlemen on the other side should flush with virtuous indignation, seeing that when they themselves were in power, they acted exactly in the same manner and instructed their agents to make the most of it in the interest of the party, for they were satisfied it was a meritorious deed, and so it was. Now, if in 1894, it was all right to act in that way, why should it be wrong in 1908? There is no sense in having double weights and double measures, even in politics. The country may reap actual benefit from a fair criticism of a government's policy; but such
criticsm, if it be unfair and carried on in a partisan spirit is always injurious.
It is desirable, to my mind, that the necessity for public works should be gauged according to a variety of circumstances, and that the government should be at liberty to help on the development of sparsely settled districts as well as that of large towns and cities. We are called upon each year to vote large sums of money for the city of Montreal, the city of Quebec, and so forth. We appropriate millions towards the development of these important centres. If among the people inhabiting these cities, there were individuals or gangs similar to those met with in Chicoutimi, who would pry into the details of these large items of expenditures, in the hope of discovering something improper, it would be an allround source of trouble and misfortune. Will my hon. friend from Saint-Antoine maintain in this House that the large expenditure of money made by the city of Montreal or by the city of Quebec could bear such severe scrutiny and unfriendly criticism as that indulged in as regards Chicoutimi? Would not such an inquiry cause the blood to curdle in the veins of so virtuous a man? Cheerfully does the House vote from year to year enormous sums towards the development of the larger cities such as Montreal and Quebec; and heretofore there has been on complaint that the House has been deceived; for we have not been called upon to listen in that connection to such petty discussions as that which has taken place yesterday. Such has been the trend of affairs since confederation be it under Liberal or Conservative rule.
My hon. friend from North Toronto, who felt so indignant yesterday, must have been apprised of the instructions given, in 1894, under the signature of the Hon. Mr. Ouimet, Minister of Public Works, for the building of two miles of a colonization road as an approach to a non-existent wharf. It seems to me that if he was in the right yesterday, he must have been previously terribly in the wrong, and his protest loses thereby a great deal of its weight.. I Tegret having to recall that circumstance, which he is unable to deny, but I have been constrained to do so. There is one important fact which strikes me in connection with this whole affair, and it is this: that informer Lapointe who is spending all his energy in ill-directed efforts to acquaint the opposition as to the state of affairs in my contitu-ency, never thinks of mentioning an extraordinary attempt at robbing the public chest, engineered by the gang, and whereby $30,000 were to be secured from the government as the price of what was called the booms of the Chicoutimi Pulp Company on the Rivef Saguenay, which booms were not



worth five cents to the government, as the hon. member for Quebec West is aware.
It was a downright fraud intended to benefit a select few only. Had the resident engineer and the chief engineer of the Public Works Department allowed themselves to be swindled out of that report, which at a certain time it was expected that they could be forced to do, in order to recommend that fraud, stupendous as was the transaction itself, these gentlemen would probably not have been treated as they were yesterday for acting conscientiously and in the public interest. The pack of boodlers who are hounding them with such hatred and cause them to be vilified before this House by well-intended members, who do not know them, would more likely perhaps leave them alone, while they busy themselves feasting upon the plunder. But the public interest of the county would have been sacrificed, and public opinion probably would not have approved of them at the last general election.

Girard had received certain sums of money, a few dollars perhaps, for services rendered the Department of Public Works ; that things have gone so far as to raise a suspicion upon the fitness of that person to carry out the work confided him, and to insinuate, to say the least, that unless that man were my son, he would not have been employed. It is all the more inexplicable that the payrolls of the Civil Service are crowded with the names of fathers, brothers, sisters, sens, cousins, step-sons, and other relatives of members of parliament, nay, of ministers, that this has been going on under all governments, Tory and Grit alike, and that nobody ever found fault with it. Why should my son be the object of such strong condemnation ? Why should he be signalled out among the throng of others, unless it be for personal vengeance, which, I am willing to admit, is not shared by my colleagues, but necessarily emanates from outside, and under the inspiration of the same crowd that I branded a while ago, and whose voice fortunately my colleagues have echoed in this House. Things have gone so far that aspersions of such a personal character have been cast upon me that I will not take them up. * I am quite willing to admit that I am not* a great manufacturer from the city of Montreal, Mr. GIRARD.
that I am not a millionaire, but I challenge every one of those who spoke yesterday on that question, to overpoise me by one single ounce in the great balance of rectitude and honour. My hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) may be wealthier than I, he may own a million, which I will never own, but as far as honour and respectability are concerned, I boast of as much wealth as he will ever have. My son, I think, worked three times for the Minister of Public Works. He was first a student at the seminary and then in the law faculty at the university. Each time he was regularly and honestly appointed by the Minister of Public Works, and not in any sneaking way by the resident engineer and myself, as was insinuated. He was one of a group of young men who were regularly appointed by the minister to conduct surveys in my district, surveys which the department needed to acquire information in answer to a great many demands by residents of the districts. Salaries were uniform for the whole staff and were fixed by the department and the minister. It has been customary, I think, for a great many years past, to help students, whoever they may be, during holidays, by teaching them piactical life and getting them used to the hardships and struggles of life, and this by having them share in some of the government works. And I thought it proper for me, without humbling or depreciating myself, especially in the light of so many precedents, to have my son benefit of this current practice.
That is what the Conservative party had done, and which is still being done by the Liberal party without anybody generally finding fault with it. As I said before, every time my son was employed, the responsible minister duly appointed him, and never to positions which he could not honestly and conscientiously fulfil with as much advantage for the minister who had so appointed him as if he had been replaced by others. I have neither shame nor. regret for what I have done, and I don't think I will ever have to repent for it. If any one thought yesterday that he was justified in suggesting anything wrong in connection with my son's appointment, I may be allowed to tell those colleagues of mine that there is as much honesty right here as can be found in them, not excepting even the hon. member for St. Antoine and that each of us individually has far more than the crowd which kept them posted in this matter.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, let me claim for my constituency, which is the largest, the youngest and the less developed in the whole Dominion, all the advantages which it is entitled to from the government and from this House. of population, such as Montreal and Quebec, for instance, but they regret every time to hear from the representatives of those cities such criticism as will stay their progress.
