I think my hon. friend knows us well enough to feel assured that nobody here enters upon that field of criticism with the desire of satisfying a personal animosity against himself. There is no man in this House, I am sure, who would be less likely to be the object of such animosity than my hon. friend himself.
Now, I wish to come to the more general question of river and harbour improvements. What I find in my experience in this House in regard to the province of Quebec is this:	We have before us this
evening, and we have had for the past twelve years, a number of items of expenditure for harbours and rivers in Quebec. Up to 1900 I, like others, proceeded to criticise these expenditures. There wa3 then before the country no complete scheme for the solution of the problem of transportation. Since I have been sitting in this committee during this session I have heard time and again ministers stating-the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) so stated two or three days ago-that this is the vital question, that this is the question above all others which we must solve and promptly solve. Since 1904 we have had the Teport of the very ablest men in this country in regard to the solution of the problem, a report that has not been called in question on either side of the House, and which has been referred to in approving terms by the government time and time again. That report dates back now four years and it contains a plan of improvements necessary and urgent from one end of the country to the other. Before that report was presented I referred with others to the necessity of certain works. What happens? You may criticise a wharf in some small place on the River St. Lawrence. I will take an example, although it is very risky work to do so. I will

take the wharf at St. Sulpice, near Montreal, and I will criticise moderately but legitimately, giving reasons for my opinion of that public work. The very next thing which the member for that county does is to give the largest degree of publicity to my criticism throughout his county. He holds meetings, denounces the opposition and points out that you have singled out this small public work, costing $8,000 or $10,000, out of animosity to the county and for the purpose of doing as much injury as possible to the county and to your own province.
I need not say that in past years my experience has been that there was a regular complicity on the part of government supporters to do as much injury as they possibly could in this way. There is another truth, and I have stated it time and again here and I will repeat it in the hope that it may obtain some publicity; I say that the member of parliament who gives no sign of existence in this House, who does not go througn the drudgery that most of us go through every day, who apparently takes no interest in what is being done for the advancement of the public business of the country, such a member undertakes as a rule to atone for that lashes on his part by endeavouring to obtain public works for his country so that he may claim that he has done something valuable and durable for his constituents. Look through the estimates any year and you will find confirmation of this. Such a man goes back to his county and he says he has done a great deal to execute the mandate that was confided to him because he has obtained a post office, or a wharf where there is no water. And what kind of a bill does the country have to foot on account of that tendency in our political life? We paid last year nearly one million dollars for works which did not advance us one single step toward the solution of the transportation problem to which I consider the country is pledged. This year we have half a million dollars spread over fifty items for improvements in the province of Quebec. I do not criticise them in detail for the reasons I have stated, but I say that the province of Quebec at the present time is more interested than any other province in the carrying out of the recommendations embodied in the report of the Transportation Commission. The Minister of Public Works tells us he is interested in that problem, and I wonder why a man like him will continue on in the same old rut that was followed, I admit, by all previous governments, although in those former days the question was not as vital as it is to-day. I wonder why the Minister of Public Works does not turn over a new leaf and begin to practise what he preaches. The report of that Transportation Commission deals with the solution of the problem from British Columbia to the Atlantic
ocean and Mr. Reford and the gentlemen associated with him on that commission, men competent beyond all question to form an opinion, stated that the port of Montreal, and the port of Quebec, and the port of St. John, and the port of Halifax should be made free national ports. They reported that it was essential that Quebec and Montreal should be immediately placed on a national basis. Here is St. Sulpice which is some distance below Montreal, and surely the district for miles around there is immensely more interested in the nationalization of the port of Montreal than in the construction of a two-penny half-penny little wharf. There are twenty counties around there which are enormously more interested in the construction of the Georgian Bay canal than they are in these small works which are invariably undertaken to please a contractor or to carry out some parochial scheme which really has nothing to do with the general interest of the surrounding country. In Montreal-and I do not speak of my own division but of Montreal and the country tributary to it extending half way down to Quebec-what is our position. We have never received a dollar from the government for the port of Montreal. True, there was a wharf built when Mr. Tarte was minister; and we have excellent harbour commissioners, but our hands are tied and we cannot go a step farther towards nationalizing the port.	And, in Montreal this year we
are going to do a thing which is exactly the contrary of what thev are doing in the United States ports; we are going- to load the port with a new burden of increased port dues in direct opposition to the recommendation of the commission of 1904, and in direct opposition to the policy pursued in the ports of Boston, Portland, New York, and Newport News, in the latter of which they are actually paying a premium to bring the traffic there. Quebec has never paid the interest on its harbour debt. It is a very important port and the people of Quebec are sending a deputation to Ottawa to lay before the government what I am now laying before the committee. The Transportation Commission reported that it was essential and urgent that we should have a dry-dock in Montreal. We have room for a dry-dock there without expropriating any property; a plan was approved by the then Minister of Public Works some years ago, but there is still no dry-dock in Montreal and our shipping is immensely hampered as a consequence. In Quebec there is no dry-dock to accommodate large vessels. A few years ago the ' Bavarian ' was salved, but she could not be kept afloat and she was hopelessly lost because not being in a condition to face an ocean voyage to an American port there was no dry-dock in which she could be repaired. Surely all these questions must ap-

i'.eal to the government. I believe if such a policy were laid before the electors of the province of Quebec in its true sense they would endorse the immediate execution of these national schemes, including as they do works which are of great moment not only to the province of Quebec but to all western Canada. We had immense shipments of grain from Montreal last year, but they could not be handled economically because the port of Montreal was not as well equipped as American ports which are its competitors. For the reasons I have stated I do not like to enter into a criticism, beyond requiring knowledge and information, of the separate items. The result to-day is that you are denounced as being against improvements in the province of Quebec. And, let the committee notice, that I do not say that any of these works is absolutely useless. There are about fifty of them. I could point out about one hundred and fifty more where bridges, wharfs, some little dredging in a river to make it navigable for batteaux would be useful and pleasant for the people. So it is difficult to say that these works are absolutely useless, although inquiry I think, will give us the information that they are carried out in a most expensive way. But I base my criticism on a higher ground, and say that at the present moment in the province of Quebec, instead of spending from $1,000,000 to $1,-
500,000	on these -small isolated works, it would be ten thousand times more beneficial to the people if we explained to them the expert opinion of the transportation problem in Canada, and why it is we must cease these small expenditures here and there and endeavour to place our province on a proper footing in Tegard to transportation.

I was wondering if 1 heard my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) aright, when he intimated that he was afraid to criticise these items lest this might be made a ground of attack upon him in the different constituencies. He will pardon me if I say that that is not what I would have expected from him as an old parliamentarian and a man of courage. I would have supposed that he would venture to do what he thought right, irrespective of local feeling or prejudices which might arise in regard to his conduct. I understood him to say that all he would venture to do would be to speak in a general way in criticism of these items, without venturing to call the attention of the committee to any special item of expenditure as being, in his opinion, not in the public interest. In my opinion, that is what our hon. friends opposite ought to do, if they think these votes ought not to be asked from parliament. If the hon. gentleman observes in these items any public work which be thinks ought not to be con-Mr. MONK.
structed in the public interest, I hold it is his duty to point that out to the committee. I would be prepared to justify the expenditure, and I say now to my hon. friend, that so far as I am aware, there is not a single public work in the province of Quebec" for which we are asking an appropriation which cannot be well justified. I am afraid that my hon. friend looks at the question of appropriations too much from the standpoint of the city in which he happens to reside. To the hon. gentleman the city of Montreal is everything, the development, the building up of that great city is everything, and he would be willing to have all the public moneys expended for the benefit of that city and other great cities, although the smaller communities in the various parts of Canada were utterly and absolutely neglected.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) will allow me to ask him in connection with what he is saying, why the government does not carry out the recommendations of the Transportation Commission in regard to the naturalization of certain ports?

The government is carrying out, just as rapidly as it can reasonably be done, the recommendations of the Transportation Commission. But let me say that, as one member of this government, and as having to do with the administration of public works, I fail to see that all other sections of the country should be sacrificed for the benefit of these great ports which are part of this great transportation system. What was the recommendation of the Transportation Commission? It was that the ports of Fort William and Port Arthur should be improved and made capable^ of rapidly assisting in the transportation of the products of the west to the eastern sections of Canada and the Atlantic seaports of our country; it was that the canal system should be deepened, that the port of Montreal should be improved, as also the ports of St. John and Halifax, and, on the Pacific coast the ports of Victoria and Vancouver.
Now, let us commence with the west and see what the government is doing. On the Fraser river, we have a powerful dredge that has been working there for some time, and another dredge in the harbour of Victoria. Within the last few months we have purchased two as good dredges as are to be found in either the Atlantic or Pacific waters of the United States. We have the * Ajax,' a very powerful dredge, and lately we purchased in Germany* a suction dredge of the most superior character, one capable of dredging to the extent of 1,000 cubic yards per hour-a thousand per cent greater capacity than the average dredge we have had working before this, a dredge with enormous capacity and one which will enable

us to do splendid work. Our idea is to make the Fraser river a great ship channel up to the city of New Westminster. We are dredging the approach to the harbour of Victoria, carrying out a definite scheme of improvement of that harbour with which the people there are well satisfied, as shown by the manner in which they expressed themselves though their board of trade and otherwise in appreciation of the work we are carrying on. In Vancouver we are entering upon the work of improving the harbour. This has not been necessary in the past, because the traffic was not congested as it has since become. We are putting on a dredge to improve the entrance to False creek, a very important part of the harbour, and we are having an examination made of the Narrows, the entrance to Bur-ard inlet, and also of the Parthia shoals and some other shoals which require to be removed. Now, coming eastward to the western shores of Lake Superior, we find that this government is to-day spending millions to make Port Arthur and Fort William capable of accommodating larger vessels which ply upon the lakes, so that the traffic of our country may be handled with as great facility as traffic is handled at Duluth. Coming eastward to the eastern shore of Georgian bay, you will find that the government, in conjunction with the two great railway companies, the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific, is developing the new harbours of Tiffin and Victoria. The railway companies are building new lines of railway almost as level as this floor, in order to divert the traffic which now goes to Buffalo and through United States ports to Canadian ports and through Canadian channels, spending on these railways no less than $50,000 to $60,000 a mile. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) will see, if he looks at the estimates, that large appropriations are made for the dredging of these ports of Victoria and Tiffin, and he will see that for Port Arthur and Fort William the magnificent sum of $600,000 is appropriated for the carrying out of this part of the great transportation scheme which the commission has recommended to the government. Now, if he comes to the port of Montreal he will find that very recently the government has expended upwards of $1,000,000 on the new pier there, and also that we are lending to the Harbour Commission of Montreal money for the purpose of carrying on vast improvements there and lending at the low rate of 3 per cent. Coming to the Atlantic sea-board, you find that so far as the port of St. John is concerned, this government has departed altogether from the policy of its predecessor, which was that no work should be done by the government in the harbour of St. John unless immediately connected with the Intercolonial. Last year the expenditure of this government at that port amounted to three-quarters of a
million. And if he will look at the estimates he will find an appropriation of $500,000 for the coming year, to carry on the work necessary to make St. John one of the great winter ports this also being a part of this great scheme of transportation. If he will go to the port of Halifax he will find great improvement there in connection with the terminus of the Intercolonial Railway. And if he will go to Quebec, he will find that we are engaged there upon works for the purpose of providing ocean terminal facilities, which will run into $2,000,000 or $3,000,000, before we get through with the very large scheme we have undertaken. If he will visit the south shores of the St. Lawrence at Levis, he will find that we have purchased there a property capable of being made into a splendid depot for our terminal, and we have an item in the estimates of $400,000 for the purpose of completing the purchase of this property and beginning the making of improvements. All along the line from the Pacific to the Atlantic, we have been moving forward to the accomplishment of the ideal which this commission had in view and recommended to the government; but while doing that, are we to sacrifice all the other sections of the country? Are we to refuse to give to the people living along the St. Lawrence in small towns and villages the accommodations in the way of wharfs and dredging which they require and the ordinary conveniencies of transportation? Let my hon. friend not forget that the trade problems of this country do not simply concern the great ports and the people inhabiting the large cities, but also the people living along the St. Lawrence and on the shores of our great lakes and the lakes and rivers of the maritime provinces, as well as the people of British Columbia, who live not alone in Vancouver, Victoria and New Westminster, but in Nanaimo and on the west coast and in many small harbours along the coast. All these people in all these sections are doing their part in contributing to the business of the small towns and cities, and these in turn are doing their part in building up the great cities of Montreal, Toronto, Quebec, St. John and Halifax. Therefore, so far as I am concerned, whilst giving attention to this great transportation problem, I am not prepared to lose sight of what might be called the smaller transportation problem, but still one which concerns many thousands of people. Take this item of St. Sulpice, and it is the only item to which my hon. friend ventured to refer. He says it might be criticised. The amount we are asking for is to repair a wharf 25 miles below Montreal, which was built by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company and which has got sadly out of repair. The people are asking us to put it in repair. That is a place of some 700 to 800 people,

principally farmers, who send a good deal of produce from there, and it would be a great loss to them if the steamers were not able to call at that wharf. We are putting that wharf in repair in order that steamers may call there and the farmers get the accommodation to which they are entitled.

My hon. friend has given a glowing description of public works generally, but the simple question I put him he has not answered. I asked why the government had not carried out the suggestion of the Transportation Commission, which called for the nationalization of the ports of Montreal and Quebec, and the building of two dry-docks, one in Montreal particularly and generally the completion within as short a delay as possible of the improvements upon the St. Lawrence route. My hon. friend says they have spent a great deal at Port Arthur and Fort William. I say that the government has not even at these points carried out the urgent recommendations of the commission which required that the government, without any delay should expropriate the water front. That was the first recommendation.
At Fort William?

The hon. minister has not answered my question. I come now to the particular instance to -which I referred. I did not state that a wharf could not be of some use at St. Sulpice. What I said was that the county in which St. Sulpice is situated and the neighbouring county were intensely more interested in the carrying out of the practical suggestions of the commission, such as the nationalization of the port of Montreal and the immediate construction of the Georgian Bay canal. These two works are of infinitely more use and benefit to St. Sulpice than the construction of a wharf. My information is that there was a wharf built by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, which does service in that locality and has done so more than half a century. Why should we interfere? Was it most urgent to make the wharf 15 feet wider? Was that as urgent as the other works to which I have referred? It was made 15 feet wider and the stones were used from the old wharf belonging to the Richelieu Company to fill up an "additional 15 feet. The work was not done by contract. If it had been, it could have been done for $3,800, but it was done by days' work, and I think we have got to pay about $7,000. Was the old Richelieu wharf purchased?
It was.
There was great dissatisfaction at St. Sulpice at the wharf being where it is? These 800 people, to whom the minister referred, were greatly dissatisfied because the wharf was not at the right
place, and in order to make things square all round, the mayor was appointed to oversee the work at $5 per day, although he knows nothing about it. He was, however, an influential man.
My hon. friend is only some 800 per cent out of the way. It was $3 instead of $5.
Is my hon. friend absolutely sure ? I think I am nearer the right figure than he.
I am sure the hon. gentleman is astray.

We want a competent man. It is not because a man is influential or is a mayor that he is particularly qualified to do the work. The wood was not called for by tender and nothing appears to have been done by tender. The wood was bought from a stone merchant, a very influential and important man to conciliate. Was it bought by tender ? I doubt it very much. That is what I have to say about the St. Sulpice improvements. I say that these people are more interested in the large works projected for transportation than in this little work for local convenience. The minister has multiplied words but he has not answered my question, why have the government not nationalized and made free the ports of Montreal and Quebec, when the Americans are competing successfully for our traffic making their ports free, equipping them for traffic and in some cases giving bonuses to the traffic?

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has declared repeatedly, to-night, that nothing had been done about dry docks at Montreal and Quebec. He even said that there was no dTy dock at Quebec.
(Translation.) I beg pardon, I never said that. I did say that the dry dock at Quebec could not hold such large ships as the ' Bavarian,' which had coused the complete wreck of that ship.

(Translation.) There is a dry dock at Quebec, which was built by the Liberal party as we all know, which cost a considerable sum of money, and has been in use until lately. Everybody knows that such undertakings are very important and cannot be brought to completion within a day's time.
I expected the hon. member for Quebec M est (Mr. Price) would contradict the statement made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
I am well aware of the fact that pressure is being brought to bear upon the government in order to induce them to comply with the wishes of the hon. gentleman. But

there is many a slip between the cup arid' the lip and the hon. gentleman will have to wait till the country is wealthy enough to accomplish the dream which haunts his sleep. When his friends were entrenched in power, they neglected to make those improvements. Public money was squandered in the port of Quebec, and that expenditure gave rise to public scandals. But it was the people's money that was spent, when those millions were being squandered, and thrown into the waters of the St. Lawrence, and what was the outcome? As all the hon. gentlemen know, it was those scandals that brought about the downfall of the party then in power
I may say that a strong agitation is being carried on by the interested parties both in Montreal and in Quebec, with a view to securing the building of dry-docks large enough to meet the actual requirements of trade. Influential delegations from Montreal and Quebec have waited upon the government and have had interviews with the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works.
With what results?

The matter has been thoroughly discussed. On the part of the government there was no such answer given as ' non expedit,' that is to^ay, nothing to show that the government were unwilling to take action. What was stated was that owing to the financial situation, and the vast public works that were being constructed, although the proposal was worthy of consideration, it was not deemed advisable for the present to start works the necessity and urgency _ of which are fully acknowledged but which could not be constructed within a short time.
All along the shores of the St. Lawrence, chiefly between Montreal and Quebec, vast improvements have been carried on; other great works are being constructed or will be resumed, during the next season. It is in the interests of Quebec and Montreal that the steamer 'Montcalm' is now busy dredging the channel between those two; cities, in order to have the river opened up to navigation earlier in the year. Those' improvements call for large expenditures which are incurred, no doubt, in the public interest, but more particularly in favour of the county which the hon. member for Jacques Cartier thinks has been sadly neglected by the government.
I do not think there has been any such neglect either in that part of the country or elsewhere. Such sweeping criticisms are calculated to lead astray public opinion and fool the people into believing that we are remiss in our duties. My hon. friend from Quebec West is well aware that such is not the case. He knows that within twelve or
eighteen months, the government are going to place at the disposal of the Minister of, Public Works with the consent of parliament the appropriations required to complete the necessary and urgent improvements in the harbours of Montreal and Quebec.
River St. Francis, St. Francis du Lac, on west side of river, $4,000.

Could the minister
give any information as to the extent to which the river is navigable at this point and the amount of navigation there is?

I am not sure as to the depth of water, but my information is that there is considerable traffic between this place and Montreal. I suppose it would be by one of the Inarket boats. I am not able to give my hon. friend the information which I suppose he would desire as to the depth of the water.
Is the minister in a position to say that there is water enough for any boat to run for more than perhaps a month in the spring time?

If the hon. gentleman asserts from personal knowledge that there is not, I will take his statement.
Mr. DOHERTY I am not asserting it; I am asking the minister for information.
I am not able to say.
It seems to me that is a matter on which we should have information before voting money.
This is to complete the work. If this were a new work I would have the details but I have not. It is to go on with the work to completion.
I cannot make any personal statement but I have information that seems to me to be reliable that it is not possible for any boats to get to that wharf except for about a month in the spring time.
What county is it in?
Yamaska.
How much is the wharf going to cost?
The total expenditure outside of the dredging will run up to about $15,000.
Is it possible for the minister to spend $15,000 where there is no navigation except for about a month in the spring?
There may not be navigation for deep draft vessels, but there is navigation for market boats.

The minister has asked me if I had personal knowledge of the

matter. I think it is a fair question to ask him if he is in a position to affirm that there is any navigation there for more than one month in the spring?

My hon. friend will see that it would be necessary for me to look up the files of the department to get that information. If this were a new work for which I was asking parliament to make an appropriation, I would have fortified myself with the reports of the engineers. But this is to continue a work to which parliament is already committed, and to which I presume parliament committed itself with all the reports before it at the time.
Would it be asking too much of the minister to fortify himself with that information for the benefit of the present parliament?
I will be glad to do so.	,
I think we ought to have the information so as to see the result of the fortification.
We have to finish the work already begun. But I will get the information and lay it on the table.
How much is the minister asking for to complete?
About $4,000.
We had an item up last night where there was no navigation. This appears to be something in the same way.
There is no suggestion of a bridge here.
I think we had better have the information before passing the item.
I may say to my hon. friend that there is an item in the supple-mentaries for the current year, upon which he can discuss this item, and in the meantime I will bring down the report.
Will the minister at the same time bring down a report in reference to the dredging that is done there in the same river?

I will make a note of it and have it brought down.
River St. Jacques (Laprairie)-ice piers near mouth on River St. Lawrence, $1,000.
This is under contract, and the item is to pay the balance of the contract.
Any bridge being erected on these piers?
No. It will protect a bridge, but there is no bridge to be built on these piers.

It is to prevent the bridge that crosses a small river from being damaged by the spring floods.
River St. Maurice-channel between Grandes Piles and Le Tuque, $15,500.
What does the minister intend to do with the dredging plant on the St. Lawrence this year ?

This amount is to continue the plant at work for the removal of boulders and improving the river generally.
River Yamaska-landing pier at St. Michel d'Yamaska, $4,500.
With regard to this wharf, will the minister furnish the same information we asked for in the other case?

Yes, I will get that, and it can be discussed at the same time with the other.
St. Alphonse (de Bagotville)-addition to wharf on south side, $25,000.

I want to take occasion on this item to say a little more upon the matter of improvements in the county of Chicoutimi and Saguenay. The hon. member (Mr. Girard) who spoke earlier this evening, was greatly grieved because he was under the impression that we made this subject a matter of personal animosity towards himself. Now I wish to assure the hon. member that so far as I am concerned I have absdlutely no animosity towards him, nor am I attacking certain items of expenditure in his county through any reason that his personality has anything to do with. I think it. is hardly fair for a member of this House to put on a sour face and to consider himself persecuted, greatly wronged and injured if members on the opposition side of the House, in fulfilling their duty, which they are sworn to perform, and in exercising their right of criticism, happen to find occasion to criticise the government and the officers of the government in respect to any item. It was no defence for the hon. member to say that these various expenditures in the county of Chicoutimi and Saguenay had the approval of the Conservatives of the county; for certainly I for one wish to go plainly on record here that whether Conservatives or Liberals in any county in the Dominion are in favour of an expenditure which I may consider to be illegal and illicit, my criticism of it would be just the same if every Conservative in the county was in favour of it. We have no objection to a county having spent in it federal money for strictly federal purposes when there has been presented in this House a statement which parliament accepts, and on which parliament votes money, and when that money is being spent as parliament agreed and intended it should be spent. Now in respect to this place, St.

Alphonse de Bagotville, we can quote another little piece of history on a par with that which we discussed in connection with the River du Moulin, another case in which the ministers have from time to time given incorrect information to this House, and in which the records of the departments have given an incorrect impression, and in which money has been voted and expended in a different way altogether from what parliament intended. An item came up in 1905 for an expenditure at St. Alphonse de Bagotville. This is the way the item was presented in the estimates :
St. Alphonse wharf-removal of rocks from approaches, $1,000.
Mr. Hyman, who was then Minister of Public Works, made this statement :
This is a large parish, and it is a small amount of money, $1,000 merely, to he spent for improving a channel.
The item passed on that recommendation. Next year the Minister of Finance had charge of the estimates, and he had an item like this in the estimates :
St. Alphonse de Bagotville, wharf repairs, $1,000.
And Mr. Fielding said:
This is to build piers in connection with the repairs to the wharf and to remove boulders from the approaches to the same. There is $1,000 in the main estimates and the total cost will be $2,000.
Evidently Mr. Fielding was under the same impression as Mr. Hyman. When the Auditor General's Report came out and showed how this money was spent this is the way the item appeared.
St. Alphonse de Bagotville, removal of rocks from approaches.
When the pay-rolls were brought down this is the way the pay-rolls read:
To remove rocks from approaches.
The explanation of Mr. Hyman and that of Mr. Fielding showed plainly that what they thought we were voting the money for was to remove the rocks from the channel and make it possible for the boats to get to the wharf. That would have been a perfectly legitimate federal expenditure. In several successive years this House was called upon to vote money for this purpose. How was that money spent? St. Alphonse de Bagotville is a town which lies at the southern end of Ha-Ha bay. The wharf has been built out into deep water, it is close up to the town of St. Alphonse de Bagotville and serves the purposes of the people of that town. I have been there and I know what I am talking about. There is a wharf to serve the purposes of the people in the town and they use it to get up the Saguenay and to keep in touch with Quebec and Tadousac.
But on the other side of the bay half a mile from where the wharf is situated there is a ridge of land that runs down into the sea and on the far side of that ridge of land there is a little hamlet called Anse a Benjamin. The people who live over in that settlement were anxious to get a road built to the wharf. They had, for a number of years, been trying to raise money to build that road. They had put some of their own money into the road, but it was necessary for the road to go up a hill 250 feet high and go down the other side. They wanted a cliff road built which will be practically a level road from Anse a Benjamin to St. Alphonse de Bagotville. They got these thousands of dollars spent year after year in blasting the rock from this road which the people of the municipality should have built for themselves. It was charged as ' removal of rocks from approaches ' and Mr. Fielding and Mr. Hyman thought it was to take out rocks in the channel to the wharf The Auditor General's Report and the pay-roll conveyed the impression that it was to take out rocks from the channel. As a matter of fact it was to build a road to a wharf that , we had_no right to build, it was not a proper federal expenditure, but it was an, expenditure which was undertaken by the people themselves, and they, having been able to get the member interested and having got the local engineer to send in a favourable report, it was built with federal money. I have photographs of it and I will be glad to send them over to the minister. He will see where the road is blasted out of the rock although this expenditure is charged to the removal of rocks from approaches.

Does not my hon. friend know that at St. Alphonse de Bagotville there aTe no rocks in the channel, that the water is very deep and that it is a place to which ocean vessels can come? I am surprised that my hon. friend should have misunderstood what the vote was for. He must have known that it was to remove rocks and make an approach to the wharf by the land.
The minister says ' to be spent for improving the channel.'
Well, Mr. Hyman was evidently misinformed. He is not the first man who has been misinformed.

I am simply surprised to see the minister get up and attempt to justify this expenditure. We voted that money for the purpose of improving navigation and yet, according to the statement of my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), it has been expended for the building of a road. I would like my hon. friend to send those photos over to the minister and ask him to justify

the statement he made to the House when he asked us to vote this money.

I can understand that on some occasions the minister might be misinformed, and I know that since I have been minister sometimes some items go through very quickly. Hon. members sometimes are not as careful about millions as at other times they are about a fifty cent piece.
We took the minister's statement as being true but we were evidently misled by him.

Evidently if the minister made that statement he was under an erroneous impression, but there was nothing in the item itself which would lead to the impression that it was to dredge out the channel because it says that it was to clear out rocks from the approach to the public wharf. It is not at all an improper expenditure to make a road leading up to a public wharf for the accommodation of the public. That has been done very frequently. The department has always made it a practice to buy the right of way to a public wharf and to improve it. There are several cases which have come under my own supervision in which I have given directions as to the approaches to public wharfs. Otherwise the wharf would be of no use. If you build a wharf you must reasonably provide an approach to it so that the public can use it. I do think that my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) ought not to be too critical with regard to an expenditure like this which was undertaken to make an approach to a wharf to give people free access to such transportation facilities as they have. They have no railways there. People in other parts of the Dominion enjoy the convenience of railways. When they go to the railway to take the train, they have a station and they can go into the waiting room and be comfortable, but in this particular locality the people, in winter time, are completely shut out from the larger- cities and in the summer time they have to depend entirely upon steamers to get their produce to market, and to go to the cities of Quebec and Montreal and other places. It was a small expenditure of $2,000.
Nearly $4,000.

The people of that place ought to have some accommodation and I do not think this expenditure is out of the way. I am sure that my hon. friend will not suggest for a single moment that either Mr. Hyman or Mr. Fielding intended to make a mis-statement to the committee because if they had asked for that vote for clearing out a roadway the committee would have granted the appropriation just as readily as though they had thought it was for another purpose.

I do not say that either Mr. Fielding or Mr. Hyman deceived parliament, but I do say that both of them were deceived by the representations that were made to them and I do say that parliament was deceived by the representations made to them. I admit that it is not a very large sum but the question is one of principle. We are deliberately being deceived in reference to these different expenditures. In this particular case, if the minister had come to us, laid down a plan and said that this money was to be expended in building a road three-quarters of a mile away from the wharf, where the wharf was right opposite _ a thriving town and thoroughly accessible to the right of way I doubt if the committee would have sanctioned it, especially as there was no more excuse for building that road three-quarters of a mile away than there was for building any other road in the county of Chicoutimi. If the minister had said: I want to build a road along the opposite side of the bay in order to connect the two hamlets do you suppose that parliament would have agreed to it?

Was it not to enable the hamlet to get to the wharf?
i Mr. AMES. It was to enable the hamlet to get to the town. Where ninety people go to the town ten people go to the wharf. It was purely to enable the people to get from the federal government what they should have done for themselves. If you had asked this House to vote that money for that purpose I guarantee you would not have got it. With that photograph in his hand, do I understand that the minister says blandly that we would have done that work for these people if they wanted it? Of course, if the minister establishes that principle then we can have no confidence whatever in the votes he proposes.

After looking at that rocky shore and looking at the approach to that wharf there I say that I believe parliament would have granted this appropriation. Look at the rock-bound shore; you would not want the people to climb down the rocks, you would say at once:	Give
them a road to the wharf. These photographs afford the strongest argument for that roadway.

I do not remember what explanations were given to the House when this appropriation was first asked, but I do know that petitions for this work were sent to me to be presented to the government. I can tell the hon. gentleman that this approach was made to get to the wharf and not to get to the town. I live in that district and I know the conditions well, and as my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) has been there once or twice in his life he no

doubt has noticed that just in front of the St. Alphonse wharf the water is about 150 feet deep and surely there would be no necessity for removing boulders there. But there is an immense hill there which prevents the people getting to that wharf and the farmers of the vicinity instead of using the St. Alphonse wharf found it better to drive, many miles out of their way to the Chicoutimi wharf. Under those circumstances the government agreed to build an approach to the wharf.
Call it a road.

Call it what you like; it is an approach to the wharf. Let me ask my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) if it is worse to make this approach to the St. Alphonse wharf which was built, than to build three miles of a road as an approach to a wharf which did not exist at all as the Conservative government did.
In what year?

About twenty years ago. When Mr. Ouimet was Minister of Public Works he contracted for the construction of three miles of road to help the settlers in canton Taillon, and nobody growled in this* House over that; no one came here. and pretended to be very much scandalized. I am much surprised that what hon. gentlemen opposite advocate to-day differs so widely from their own practices when they were in power. The difference between this government and the Conservative government is that the Liberal government built an approach to a wharf at St. Alphonse where there is a wharf actually in existenec, and the Conservative government built an approach to a wharf at Taillon where there was no wharf at all. I understand that my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) is fond of taking photographs.
And I use them to good purpose.
I hope so, but I regret very much that the only place he seems to be in the photographing business is in the Chicoutimi district.
I have lots of others.

I believe if the hon. gentleman is honest he will tell us that he does not bring this matter up on his own initiative; he knows very well that somebody else is at the bottom of it, who I can tell him is not a friend of his although he may think he is. I register my protest against that. These people have not courage enough to authorize the hon. .gentleman to give their names here when they come hypocritically attacking the government and myself and trying to make the House believe that nothing but crooked business is done in my district, and that the government is always wrong when it
does anything for my constituents. I am glad the hon. gentleman declared that he had nothing personal against me.
Nothing personal against you at all.

I want the hon. gentleman to understand that he is the instrument of some one who has personal malice against me, and I would remind him that of all those employed by the government on that work the only name to be selected was that of my son. How did my hon. friend get on to that unless some one pointed it out to him? Does not that show personal malice? I know very well that the hon. gentleman never himself knew that L. P. Girard was my son, but I know that Mr. Lapointe came here to give him the information to try to make trouble for me. I invite the hon. gentleman to inquire about Mr. Lapointe. I know what kind of a man he is, and I know he is making all that trouble because he has now suits in the courts against him because during the election he attacked the government and he attacked myself and he attacked the employees of the government and called us all robbers. He now has got himself into a corner and he wants to try and save his own skin by attacking me. I thought my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) was so high that he would not descend so low as to bring such matters before the House.
Ste. Anne des Monts, harbour improvements at mouth of Grande riviere, Ste. Anne, $2,500.
What is the explanation of this?

This is to construct certain works at this point and if the object is accomplished it will make quite a safe and commodious boat harbour for small vessels in that part of the St. Lawrence. The total estimated cost is $17,750, and this I think will complete the work.
St. Fulgence wharf, $1,000.
How much more is going to be spent on this wharf?
This is to complete.
Does the minister state definitely that this will complete the work?

The minister states that just as definitely as one can relying upon thoroughly competent engineers; oh, yes, this will complete.
St. Jean des Chaillons wharf, including dredging, $3,500.
When was that work commenced ?

About eight or ten
months ago.
That is, it began about June ?

Yes.
Mr. AMES'. When was it discontinued ?

This is to make further provision for the work which includes dredging in front of the wharf to clear away the spoil material removed from the St. Lawrence ship channel, apparently dumped there through the carelessness of those operating the dredges. A depth of only ten feet of water has been left at a distance of 85 feet north of the new structure, where there was a depth of over 16 feet. We are also prolonging the side wharfing commencing at the foot of the cliff, and constructing on its slope a retaining wall of open-face cedar crib-work to prevent the earth and trees from sliding into the river, and obstructing the present roadway leading down to the wharf.
The minister has not answered my question. He says the work began ten months ago. When did it cease ?

I can tell the hon. member (Mr. Ames) the work that has been done, but I cannot tell the exact date when it was discontinued. I suppose it was discontinued at the close of the season. The work done during eight months included building about 110,000 feet Of open-face cribwork of which 160 feet in length of side of the wharf averaging 6 feet high, 30 to 33 feet wide on 137 feet and 18 to 20 feet on 23 feet. Of the protection wall there was built 99 feet in length by 12 feet in height, and partly filled up with stone ballast to secure its stability. To overcome the steep elevation of the hill, ascending towards the public highway, a crib of openfaced work was erected on the east end of the wharf, its dimensions at base being 29 x 33 feet rising up to 29 feet with 2J feet batter on side, giving it a 24 foot square platform on top, extending and working backwards into the cliff as it worked upwards. A trestle roadway of 76 feet by 24 at platform and 44 at upper end is to connect with road on hilltop.

What I want to know, if the minister can tell me is, when this work commenced, and when it ceased. Here is a case where the county is not getting justice, if my information is correct. Instead of opposing this work, I am asking that it be gone on with in earnest. If my information is correct, this work was commenced about a week before the provincial general election-that is it was commenced on the 1st of June. And, as soon as the elections were over, say on the 10th of June, the work was discontinued. Again it was taken up a short time before the Dominion elections in October, and when they were over it was again discontinued. The work should be taken up and finished, Mr. AMES.
instead of being gone on with only when there happens to be an election.

I think, perhaps, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) has in mind the work on the roadway. During the harvest season it is hard to get labouring people to leave their farms, but later in the season they could easily go on with this work. It happened, perhaps unfortunately, that the elections came on shortly after harvest, when the men could leave their farms without disadvantage. But I think that what the hon. gentleman says would not apply to what might be called the wharf work, which I think, went on pretty continuously. The hon. gentleman, then, agrees with me that it is a very necessary work, does he not?

The hon minister (Mr. Pugs-ley) pays the climate of Quebec a great compliment when he suggests that the harvest season commences on June 10, and that it was necessary to take the men off the work on the roadway two days after the election.
I was speaking of the harvest in August and September.
The minister had better try to get another excuse; this one is very thin.
Strange to say, at this moment, I cannot do better than that.
Perhaps the hon. minister will bring down the pay-sheets when he brings the other information.
I will bring everything; I will get an ox cart and bring everything down.

Here is a case, where again, you are playing with a public work, taking it up when a provincial or federal election comes on, doing a little work, and then dismissing the men when the election is over. If the work is worth doing, do it; if it is not worth doing, do not make a pretense of doing it merely because an election is coming on.
St. Nicholas-repairs to wharf, &c., $2,850.
Is the St. Nicholas wharf leased, and if so, to whom, and at what price?
I have no record of any lease.
In the Auditor General's Report the minister will see it stated that it has been leased at $25 a year. To whom?
That would be by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Did we build it with a view to leasing it to some one? If so, to whom?

As my hon. friend, perhaps, knows, my department does not col-

lect revenue for wharfs, but if we transfer to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, it collects tolls, or, it may perhaps give relief from tolls-I am not quite sure. If there were any lease, it would be a matter entirely in the Marine Department. I have no knowledge of it.
There was $3,000 voted last year.
Yes, this is a revote of $2,850.
What was done with the $150?

There was a little work
done.
At election time ?
There was some planking done with that.
The question to my mind is whether we have built that wharf in order that it might be leased to private parties, and in that case whether the public still have rights to the wharf?
The public have complete rights on the wharf. It is against the policy of the government to give exclusive privileges to any one.
Was the expenditure incurred in order to lease it to some party at $25 per year ?
Where does my hon. friend get that information that it is leased ?
In the Auditor General's Report.

If my hon. friend will look closer, he will see that that is simply the revenue derived from the steamboat company which, instead of paying tolls on goods landed at each trip, pays an annual charge. The wharf is open to all who wish to use it.
Sorel-deep water wharf, $86,000.
Is that the wharf which turned over last summer ?

No, the wharf which turned over was built some years ago. We are rebuilding the wharf but upon a different design, and after making very careful examination of the bed of the river, we are quite satisfied the wharf we are now building will stand. The sub-soil there is very shifty in its character, there is a good deal of quick sand, and having tested the foundation, we are building a different substructure altogether.
Some resolutions reported.
What business to-moT-row ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We contemplated proceeding with the loan resolutions of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but as some information desired by hon. gentlemen opposite is not quite ready, we will postpone that matter until Tuesday. To-morrow the House will be moved into Committee of Supply, and the estimates taken up. I move that the House do now adjourn.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.
Friday, March 19, 1909.
